title: Do Newcomers Have to Become Jewish?
overview: The early followers of Jesus argue over whether believers who are not Jewish must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, and their leaders in Jerusalem decide they do not.

parts.label: Trouble in Antioch (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Visitors from Judea told the mostly non Jewish believers in Antioch that they had to be circumcised, the ancient sign of belonging to God's people under Moses' law, or they could not be saved. Paul and Barnabas strongly disagreed, so the church sent them to Jerusalem, where some believers from the Pharisees, a group known for strict keeping of the law, made the same demand.

parts.label: Peter's argument (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: Peter reminds the leaders of the time God gave the Holy Spirit to a household that was not Jewish, before anyone was circumcised (told in chapter 10). He calls the law a yoke, a heavy load even Jews struggled to carry, and says Jews and others alike are saved the same way, by the undeserved kindness of Jesus.

parts.label: James and the prophets (vv. 12-18)
parts.note: After Paul and Barnabas describe what happened among other nations, James, the leader of the Jerusalem church and usually identified as Jesus' brother, speaks. He quotes the prophet Amos about God rebuilding David's fallen tent, reading it to mean that God's restored people would include other nations, as something God had planned long ago.

parts.label: Four simple requests (vv. 19-21)
parts.note: James rules that these believers should not be burdened with the whole law, only asked to avoid food offered to idols, sexual immorality, meat from strangled animals, and blood. Many scholars think these echo rules for foreigners living among Israel in Leviticus 17 and 18, meant to let Jewish and other believers share meals and life, since Moses' law was read in every town.

parts.label: The letter goes out (vv. 22-35)
parts.note: The leaders send a letter with Judas and Silas saying the earlier visitors had no authority from them, and listing only the four requests. The believers in Antioch were relieved and glad, and the messengers stayed a while to encourage them.

parts.label: Paul and Barnabas part ways (vv. 36-41)
parts.note: Paul refuses to take Mark on a new trip because Mark had left them partway through the last one, and the quarrel is so sharp the two partners separate. The book does not say who was right, though Paul's later letters speak warmly of Mark.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the four requests were a temporary compromise to help Jewish and other believers live together, or lasting rules still binding today, which is why a few groups still avoid eating blood.
think: When a group welcomes newcomers, how would you tell which of its customs are truly essential to belonging and which are simply familiar habits?
